significance.justification: A verified-true result would establish a form-(iii) law: language-ID decodability follows a "U-shaped layer profile," varies inversely with content decodability, cross-lingual editing success peaks at the trough, and "deeper/wider trough -> better transfer." This would constrain expected layer orderings, intervention outcomes, and transfer behavior across model sizes; that is materially weightier than merely locating a language-neutral middle, the issue highlighted by Wendler et al., "Do Llamas Work in English? On the Latent Language of Multilingual Transformers" (2024). It establishes both a phenomenon and a proposed mechanism, while a negative result would rule out the unified life-cycle account, although failure of only one coupling would not by itself identify the replacement mechanism. True and false are distinguishable through the stated ordering and couplings, and the topic-substitution check lowers no score: the topic alone does not imply this U-shape, causal alignment, or trough-to-transfer prediction.

reach.justification: The named handles are "trough layer and depth" and the resulting "principled target layer for cross-lingual interventions," plus a proposed predictor of transfer quality from trough width and depth. These are ex ante handles after calibration: they can select an editing or patching layer and potentially forecast transfer before the downstream intervention or deployment outcome. Re-extraction on a new model would not merely restart an open search, because the asserted relations predict another U-shaped curve, maximal intervention success at its trough, and better transfer for a deeper or wider trough; however, scope is limited mainly to multilingual models across sizes, with no explicit law for architecture changes, language distance, or interference. Downstream users include multilingual-model researchers and potentially auditors choosing intervention layers, and the topic-substitution check passes because those transferable relations and handles disappear when the claim is replaced by the generic multilingual-representation topic.
